```{r}
  geom_line(data = mc_range, aes(x = conc, y = typical), colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = mc_curves, aes(x = conc, y = uptake, linetype = plant), colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(
    data = mc_points,
    aes(x = conc, y = uptake, shape = plant),
    colour = "#0072B2",
    alpha = 0.7,
    size = 2
  ) +
  labs(
    x = expression("Ambient CO"[2] * " concentration (µL/L)"),
    y = expression("CO"[2] * " uptake (µmol/m²/s)"),
    linetype = "Plant",
    shape = "Plant"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {#imp-stand-growth .callout-important title="sapling growth in forest stands"}

The height growth of saplings is described with a model in which the typical growth rate
of stand $j$ is $r\,e^{u_j}$, with $u_j\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,\sigma^2_{\mathrm{stand}})$.
The estimates are $r=20$ cm/year and $\sigma_{\mathrm{stand}}=0.4$. Between which values
lie the typical growth rates of 95% of new stands? A stand that was surveyed has a predicted
effect of 0.5: what is its typical growth rate, and which of the two answers would you use
to plan a planting in a stand that was not surveyed? Is the mean growth rate over stands
20 cm/year? Calculate it in R by simulating many stands.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The range is $20\,e^{-1.96\times0.4}\approx9.1$ to $20\,e^{1.96\times0.4}\approx43.8$
cm/year, which is wide because $\sigma_{\mathrm{stand}}$ is large. The surveyed stand has a
typical growth rate of $20\,e^{0.5}\approx33.0$ cm/year. That value describes this stand
only; for a stand that was not surveyed we know only the distribution of stand effects, so
we expect a typical growth rate of 20 cm/year, anywhere between about 9 and 44 cm/year. The
mean growth rate over stands is larger than 20 cm/year, because 20 cm/year is the median:
the exponential stretches the stands above the median more than it compresses those below.
In R:

```{r}
# Range of the typical growth rates of new stands (cm/year).
20 * exp(qnorm(p = c(0.025, 0.975)) * 0.4)

# Mean over many simulated stands (cm/year).
set.seed(seed = 702)
mean(20 * exp(rnorm(n = 1e6, mean = 0, sd = 0.4)))
```

The mean growth rate over stands is about 21.6 cm/year, 8% above the median.

:::
::::

# Checking a grouped model {#sec-grouped-residuals}

A fitted grouped model is a data generating process with two levels: first the effects of
the groups are drawn from their distribution, and then the observations are drawn for
these effects. Checking the model means comparing data simulated in this way with the
observations, with scaled quantile residuals as in
[Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd#sec-response-residuals). The observations are marked
with `OBS()` in the NLL, and `obj$simulate()` then draws both levels: new effects for all
the groups, and new observations for these effects. This is called **unconditional
simulation**, because the effects of the groups are not kept at their predicted values.
RTMB simulates in the order of the lines of the NLL. At the line with the density of the
random effects it draws new values of them, and the lines below use these values, which is
why the density of the random effects must come before the lines that use them. (Keeping
the effects at their predicted values instead, **conditional simulation**, simulates new
observations of the same groups; it checks the curves of the observed groups and not the
distribution of group effects.)

For the CO₂ data the NLL with origin and chilling gains one line, `uptake = OBS(uptake)`.
We process it and fit it again (the estimates do not change):

```{r}
# The NLL with origin and chilling, with one more line.
treatment_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Mark the response as observations, so that they can be simulated.
  uptake = OBS(uptake)
  sd_plant = exp(log_sd_plant)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = sd_plant, log = TRUE))
  log_a = X_asym %*% beta_asym + u
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_rate)
  sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs)
  log_typical = X_asym_group %*% beta_asym
  log_chill_factor = log_typical[c(2, 4)] - log_typical[c(1, 3)]
  ADREPORT(log_chill_factor)
  mu = a[plant] * (1 - exp(-b * (conc - c0)))
  nll - sum(dnorm(x = uptake, mean = mu, sd = sd_obs, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL and fit it again.
treatment_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(treatment_nll, co2_data),
  list(
    beta_asym = c(log(30), rep(0, ncol(X_asym) - 1)),
    log_rate = log(0.01), c0 = 50,
    log_sd_plant = log(0.1), log_sd_obs = log(2), u = rep(0, 12)
  ),
  random = "u",
  silent = TRUE
)
treatment_fit = optim(
  par = treatment_obj$par,
  fn = treatment_obj$fn,
  gr = treatment_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
treatment_fit$convergence
```

Each call to `simulate()` returns a list with new deviations `u` for the 12 plants and new
measurements `uptake` for the 84 rows. We keep the measurements of 1,000 hypothetical
samples in a matrix with one row per measurement:

```{r}
# 1,000 hypothetical samples: new plant deviations, then new measurements for them.
n_sim = 1000
treatment_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = length(co2_data$uptake), ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 701)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  treatment_simulations[, j] = treatment_obj$simulate(treatment_fit$par)$uptake
}
```

The expected value of a measurement before its plant deviation is known is the typical
curve of the origin and treatment of its plant, so that is what we give DHARMa as
`fittedPredictedResponse`. The typical log asymptote of each plant is its row of the model
matrix `X_asym` times the estimates. The uptake is continuous, so `integerResponse` keeps
its default value. The residuals of the 84 measurements are:

```{r}
#| label: fig-residuals_grouped
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals of the 84 measurements under the model with a random asymptote and the effects of origin and chilling, from 1,000 hypothetical samples with new plant deviations, as drawn by DHARMa. Left: quantile–quantile plot against a uniform distribution. Right: residuals against the rank of the typical curve of each measurement, with the quartiles of a uniform distribution (dashed lines) and lines fitted to the quartiles of the residuals."
# Typical asymptote (u = 0) of each plant, then the expected uptake of each measurement
# on the typical curve of its plant's origin and treatment.
typical_asym = exp(drop(X_asym %*% beta_asym_mle))
treatment_expected = typical_asym[co2_data$plant] *
  (1 - exp(-exp(treatment_par[["log_rate"]]) * (co2_data$conc - treatment_par[["c0"]])))

# Scaled quantile residuals and the two standard panels.
treatment_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = treatment_simulations,
  observedResponse = co2_data$uptake,
  fittedPredictedResponse = treatment_expected
)
plot(treatment_residuals)
```

The quantile–quantile plot follows the line, and the dispersion statistic is below one:

```{r}
# Observed spread around the typical curves relative to the simulated spread.
DHARMa::testDispersion(treatment_residuals, plot = FALSE)$statistic
```

The measurements vary around their typical curves about 80% as much (as a variance) as in
the simulated samples. Most of this variation comes from the deviations of 12 plants, which
vary a lot from one hypothetical sample to the next, so this is not a clear disagreement. In
the right panel the line of the upper quartile lies above 0.75, most of all at low typical
values, and DHARMa marks it in red. Many of the measurements with low typical values
belong to the chilled plants from Mississippi, and the residuals of Mc1 and Mc3 are mostly
high, because the seven
measurements of a plant share its deviation and both plants lie above the typical curve
(@fig-new_plants). The 84 residuals are therefore not 84 independent values, and a pattern
among them can come from a few plants and not from the shape of the curve. As in Chapter
6, we read the plots and the dispersion statistic as exploratory evidence, and not the
tests that DHARMa prints with them.

The residuals of the groups themselves come from `DHARMa::recalculateResiduals()`, whose
argument `group` gives the group of each observation. It adds up the observed values of
each group, and the simulated values of each group in each hypothetical sample, and
calculates one residual per group from these sums. The function `residuals()` returns the
scaled quantile residuals of a DHARMa object, and we name them by plant:

```{r}
# One residual per plant, from the sums of its seven measurements.
plant_residuals = DHARMa::recalculateResiduals(treatment_residuals, group = co2_data$plant)
plant_scaled = residuals(plant_residuals)
names(plant_scaled) = plant_names
round(plant_scaled, 3)
```

The residual of Mc2 is 0.010: its total uptake is lower than in 99% of the simulated
plants of its origin and treatment, so its asymptote is lower than the model expects for
such a plant, as @fig-new_plants showed. Among 12 plants one residual this extreme is not
unusual, so this is a pattern to note, not a sign that the model fails. With more plants
in this group, several of them in the tails would suggest that the distribution of plant
effects should be wider or have a longer tail than the Normal distribution allows.

::: {.callout-warning title="Residuals of observations and of groups"}
A grouped model can disagree with the data at either level, and the residuals of one level
can hide a problem at the other. Residuals of the observations mix the deviation of their
group with their own variation, so a curve that misses some groups may look acceptable, and
a pattern that looks like a misfit of the curve may come from a few groups. Residuals of
the groups summarise each group in one number, so they cannot show a problem with the
shape of the curve within groups. Check both. With few groups, as here, a quiet plot of
the group residuals says little about whether the distribution of group effects is Normal.
:::

# Comparing grouped models {#sec-grouped-comparison}

Grouped models are compared with AIC
([Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-aic)) calculated from the maximum marginal
log-likelihood. $K$ counts the parameters that were estimated, the fixed effects and the
variance parameters, but not the random effects, which were integrated out: the
deviations of the 12 plants cost one parameter, $\sigma_{\mathrm{plant}}$, and not 12. The
vector `par` of a fit holds exactly these parameters, so $K$ is its length. A model
without random effects is the special case $\sigma_{\mathrm{group}}=0$, which lies at the
boundary of the range of the parameter, where the large-sample theory behind AIC does not
hold, so a comparison between models with and without random effects is only an
approximate guide.

AICc and BIC need the number of independent observations $n$, and for grouped data it is
ambiguous. The 84 measurements are not independent, because the measurements of a plant
share its deviation, but they are not only 12 observations either, because each
measurement adds information about the curve of its plant. The effective number lies
somewhere between the number of groups and the number of observations, and depends on how
large the variance among groups is compared with the variance within groups. So we do not
use AICc and BIC for grouped models, and compare them with AIC.

Four candidates answer three questions: do the plants differ at all, do origin and
chilling explain part of the differences, and does the effect of chilling depend on the
origin? Besides the
three models already fitted (complete pooling, the random asymptote, and the random
asymptote with origin, chilling and their interaction), we fit the random asymptote with
origin and chilling but no interaction. With a model matrix, the three candidates with
plant deviations differ only in their formulas, and they share the NLL `treatment_nll`:
the formula `~ 1` gives a model matrix with the column `(Intercept)` only, which is the
random asymptote without predictors, `~ Type + Treatment` gives origin and chilling
without their interaction, and `~ Type * Treatment` the model of @sec-group-predictors.
Complete pooling has no plant deviations, so it needs an NLL of its own. We write it with
a model matrix as well, so that it goes through the same bookkeeping as the other
candidates below; with the formula `~ 1` it is the model of @sec-pooling:

```{r}
# Complete pooling with a model matrix for the log asymptote: no plant deviations.
pooled_matrix_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  log_a = X_asym %*% beta_asym
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_rate)
  sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs)
  mu = a[plant] * (1 - exp(-b * (conc - c0)))
  -sum(dnorm(x = uptake, mean = mu, sd = sd_obs, log = TRUE))
}
```

As in Chapter 6, we collect the candidates in a list, each with its NLL, its formula and
whether it has plant deviations:

```{r}
# The NLL and the formula of each candidate, and whether it has plant deviations.
models = list(
  pooled = list(nll = pooled_matrix_nll, formula = ~ 1, random = FALSE),
  mixed = list(nll = treatment_nll, formula = ~ 1, random = TRUE),
  additive = list(nll = treatment_nll, formula = ~ Type + Treatment, random = TRUE),
  treatment = list(nll = treatment_nll, formula = ~ Type * Treatment, random = TRUE)
)
```

Three short functions do the bookkeeping for a candidate:

- `formula_data()` makes the list of data of a formula: the measurements, taken from a
  list of data such as `co2_data`, and the model matrices of the plants and of the four
  combinations of origin and treatment, built from the data frames `plant_info` and
  `group_info` that it receives as arguments, as in @sec-model-matrix;
- `start_values()` makes the starting values: $\log(30)$ for the baseline and zero for the
  other columns of the model matrix, so that a change of formula needs no change of code,
  and one deviation per plant in the data when the model has plant deviations;
- `fit_model()` processes the NLL of a candidate for a list of data, with `random = "u"`
  when the model has plant deviations, and fits it.

```{r}
# List of data for a formula: the measurements, and the model matrices of the plants and
# of the four combinations of origin and treatment.
formula_data = function(formula, data, plant_info, group_info) {
  list(
    conc = data$conc,
    uptake = data$uptake,
    plant = data$plant,
    X_asym = model.matrix(formula, data = plant_info),
    X_asym_group = model.matrix(formula, data = group_info)
  )
}

# Starting values of a candidate, with one coefficient per column of the model matrix and
# one deviation per plant in the data if it has plant deviations.
start_values = function(model, data) {
  start = list(
    beta_asym = c(log(30), rep(0, ncol(data$X_asym) - 1)),
    log_rate = log(0.01),
    c0 = 50
  )
  if (model$random) {
    c(start, list(log_sd_plant = log(0.1), log_sd_obs = log(2), u = rep(0, nrow(data$X_asym))))
  } else {
    c(start, list(log_sd_obs = log(2)))
  }
}

# Fit one candidate to one list of data, integrating out the plant deviations if it has
# them.
fit_model = function(model, data) {
  random = NULL
  if (model$random) {
    random = "u"
  }
  obj = MakeADFun(
    cmb(model$nll, data), start_values(model, data), random = random, silent = TRUE
  )
  optim(par = obj$par, fn = obj$fn, gr = obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
}
```

A loop fits the four candidates to the 84 measurements and calculates their AIC and its
difference from the lowest AIC:

```{r}
# Fit every candidate to the 12 plants; K is the number of estimated parameters.
comparison = data.frame(model = names(models), K = NA, loglik = NA, convergence = NA)
for (m in seq_along(models)) {
  candidate_data = formula_data(models[[m]]$formula, co2_data, plant_info, group_info)
  fit = fit_model(models[[m]], candidate_data)
  comparison$K[m] = length(fit$par)
  comparison$loglik[m] = -fit$value
  comparison$convergence[m] = fit$convergence
}
comparison$aic = 2 * comparison$K - 2 * comparison$loglik
comparison$delta_aic = comparison$aic - min(comparison$aic)
comparison
```

All four fits converged. AIC prefers the random asymptote with origin, chilling and their
interaction. The model without the interaction is worse by 8.6 units, so the data support
an effect of chilling that differs between the two origins, and the random asymptote
without predictors is worse by 25.0 units, so origin and chilling explain a large part of
the differences among the plants. Complete pooling comes last, 175 units above the random
asymptote without predictors. It lies at the boundary $\sigma_{\mathrm{plant}}=0$, so this
difference is only an approximate guide, but one of this size leaves no doubt that the
plants differ. Whether they still differ once their origin and treatment are known is a
question that this comparison cannot answer, because every candidate with origin and
chilling also has plant deviations. The likelihood profile interval of
$\sigma_{\mathrm{plant}}$ in @sec-grouped-uncertainty answers it: plants of the same
origin and treatment differ by between about 5% and 14%, and values near zero lie outside
the interval.

No pooling is not in the table. Its AIC, 372.9, is lower than that of every mixed model,
but it answers another question. Its likelihood describes new measurements of the same 12
plants, with their 12 asymptotes as parameters, whereas the marginal likelihood of a mixed
model describes the measurements of a new plant, whose asymptote is unknown. The two
likelihoods are probabilities of different things, so their AICs cannot be compared.

For the ecological question we use the model with the interaction. Chilling multiplies the
typical uptake capacity of plants from Quebec by about 0.90 (Wald interval from the log
scale 0.79 to 1.03) and that of plants from Mississippi by about 0.59 (0.52 to 0.68), and
the ratio of the two factors lies between 0.53 and 0.81 (likelihood profile interval).
So a cold night hardly affects the plants from the colder origin, and lowers the capacity
of the plants from the warmer origin by about two fifths. Plants of the same origin and
treatment differ by roughly 8% (5% to 14%), or 10% when the variance is estimated by REML.
With three plants per combination, these conclusions rest on 12 plants, which is why the
intervals of the effects and of the variance among plants are wide.

# A recipe for a grouped response curve {#sec-grouped-recipe}

The steps of this chapter extend the recipe of [Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd) to
observations that come in groups:

::: {.callout-note title="A recipe for a grouped response curve"}
1. Identify the observational unit and the groups, and whether each predictor is measured
   on the observations or on the groups. Build the model matrix of the predictors with
   `model.matrix()`, from a formula and a data frame with one row per group (or per
   observation), and check the reference level of each factor.
2. Choose the curve and the observation model as in Chapter 6, and the parameter of the
   curve that varies among groups, on a scale on which a Normal deviation is plausible
   (the logarithm of a positive parameter, the logit of a probability).
3. Write the joint NLL: minus the log density of the random effects first, then minus the
   log density of the observations for given random effects.
4. Process it with `MakeADFun()` and `random`, with one starting value of zero per group,
   fit it with `optim()`, and check that `convergence` is zero.
5. Read the variance components and the predicted group effects from `sdreport()`, and
   calculate likelihood profile intervals with `TMB::tmbprofile()` for the parameters that
   the question is about, including the log standard deviations; fit the model by REML as
   well when the variance components are the question.
6. Draw the curves of the observed groups, the typical curve and the range of new groups,
   and use each for the question that it answers.
7. Mark the response with `OBS()`, simulate hypothetical samples with `obj$simulate()`, and
   check the scaled quantile residuals of the observations and of the groups.
8. Compare the candidate models, fitted by maximum likelihood to the same observations,
   with AIC; candidates that differ only in their fixed effects share one NLL and differ
   in their formulas.
9. Interpret the fixed effects and the variance among groups in units, in terms of the
   ecological question, and say what the number of groups leaves uncertain.
:::

# Summary

Observations that come in groups share the conditions of their group, so they are not
independent. A grouped model describes this with two levels: the effects of the groups
follow a distribution, and the observations follow a distribution for given values of
these effects. The observations of a group are then independent for a given effect of
their group but dependent marginally. The parameters shared by all groups are fixed
effects, the deviations of the groups are random effects, and the model is a mixed-effects
model. Complete pooling ignores the groups, no pooling gives each group parameters of its
own, and partial pooling, the mixed model, describes both the measured groups and groups in
general.

The likelihood of a mixed model is the marginal likelihood, with the random effects
integrated out, and RTMB approximates the integral with the Laplace approximation when
`MakeADFun()` is given the argument `random`. The NLL that we write is the joint NLL, with
the density of the random effects first. The variance components describe the variation
among groups and within groups; predicted group effects are shrunk towards the typical
value of groups with the same predictors, more so for groups with few or imprecise
observations. Group-level predictors explain part of the variation among groups, and the
variance component then describes the variation that remains. They enter the NLL through a
model matrix, which `model.matrix()` builds from a formula, with one row per group and one
column per coefficient; the first level of each factor is the reference level, and the
formula interfaces of R build the same matrix.

A variance among groups is estimated from the groups, so with few groups its interval is
wide; likelihood profile intervals on the log scale of the standard deviation are the
reference. Maximum likelihood estimates of variances tend to be too small, and REML, which
integrates the fixed effects out as well, reduces this bias, but REML fits are not used to
compare models with different fixed effects. The curve of an observed group, the typical
curve and the range of new groups answer different questions.

A grouped model is checked by unconditional simulation, with residuals of the observations
and of the groups, each of which can hide what the other shows. Grouped models are
compared with AIC on the marginal likelihood, with $K$ counting the variance parameters and
not the random effects; AICc and BIC are not used, because the number of independent
observations is ambiguous.

The likelihoods of the CO₂ data were maximised without difficulty, but the practical meets
fits that stop before the maximum. In [Chapter 8](../Chapter_8/Theory.qmd) we look at how
optimisers work, and at what to do when they fail to find the maximum of a likelihood.

# Chapter quiz

The questions below follow the order of the chapter. Try each question before opening its
solution.

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 1: bats at roosts"}

The number of bats leaving each of 15 roosts is counted on 10 nights per roost. What is the
observational unit, and what is the group? What goes wrong if the 150 counts are treated as
independent observations?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The observational unit is one count, on one night at one roost, and the group is the
roost. Counts at the same roost share its size and surroundings, so they resemble each
other more than counts at different roosts. Treated as independent, the 150 counts would
be taken as more informative than they are: the standard errors of effects that vary
among roosts would be too small, the intervals too narrow, and the evidence for such
effects would look stronger than it is.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 2: nest predation and rodent years"}

A year is a rodent year with probability 0.3. In a rodent year a nest is predated with
probability 0.6, in other years with probability 0.2. What is the marginal probability
that a nest is predated? What is the probability that the year was a rodent year, for a
given predated nest?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The marginal probability adds the joint probabilities over the two kinds of year:
$0.3\times0.6+0.7\times0.2=0.18+0.14=0.32$. The conditional probability is the joint
probability divided by the marginal probability of the given value:
$0.18/0.32\approx0.56$. A predated nest makes a rodent year more probable (0.56 against
0.3), which is how the nests of one year come to be dependent when the kind of year is
not known.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 3: fish growth in lakes"}

The growth curves of fish are measured in 10 lakes. Which model, complete, no or partial
pooling, answers each question: (a) which of these 10 lakes has the fastest growth; (b) how
much growth varies among lakes of the region; (c) which growth curve to expect in a lake
that was not sampled? What does complete pooling assume?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

(a) No pooling or partial pooling: both give each lake its own curve, and partial pooling
shrinks the curves of lakes with few fish. (b) and (c) Partial pooling only, because only
it describes how lakes vary: its variance among lakes answers (b), and its typical curve
with the range of new lakes answers (c). Complete pooling assumes that the lakes do not
differ, so it answers none of these questions.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 4: body mass of lizards"}

The body mass of 30 lizards is weighed several times during a season, and a model with a
random effect per lizard is fitted. What do $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{lizard}}$ and
$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$ describe? Would weighing each lizard more often give a more
precise estimate of $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{lizard}}$?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{lizard}}$ is the variance among lizards of their typical mass (on the
scale of the random effect), and $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$ the variance of repeated
weighings of one lizard around its own typical mass, which includes changes during the
season and the error of the scale. More weighings determine the mass of each lizard better
and $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$ more precisely, but $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{lizard}}$ is a
variance among 30 lizards, and its precision is limited by the number of lizards. To
estimate it more precisely, weigh more lizards.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 5: grazing at grassland sites"}

The plant cover of quadrats at 30 grassland sites is modelled with a random effect per site
on the log of the typical cover. A site-level factor `grazing`, created with `factor()` from
the values `"none"`, `"light"` and `"heavy"`, enters through
`model.matrix(~ grazing, data = sites)`, with one row per site. Which columns does the
model matrix have, and what does each coefficient mean? How would you make the ungrazed
sites the baseline? What would change if `grazing` were an ordered factor?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

`factor()` puts the levels in alphabetical order, `"heavy"`, `"light"`, `"none"`, so the
reference level is heavy grazing. The columns are `(Intercept)`, `grazinglight` and
`grazingnone`: the first coefficient is the typical log cover of heavily grazed sites, and
the other two are the differences in typical log cover of lightly grazed and of ungrazed
sites from heavily grazed ones.
`sites$grazing = relevel(sites$grazing, ref = "none")` makes the ungrazed sites the
baseline, with the columns `grazingheavy` and `grazinglight`; the model, its maximum
likelihood and its fitted values stay the same, and only the meaning of the coefficients
changes. An ordered factor would get polynomial contrasts, with the columns `grazing.L` and
`grazing.Q` for linear and quadratic trends across the levels, which are not differences
from a reference level; `factor(sites$grazing, ordered = FALSE)` converts it back.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 6: lichen cover on rocks"}

In a model for the lichen cover of quadrats on rocks, with a random effect per rock, the
variance among rocks is estimated close to zero. What happens to the predicted effects of
the rocks, and what does the model then resemble?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The distribution of rock effects then says that rocks are alike, so every predicted effect
is shrunk almost completely to zero, whatever the observations of the rock. The model is
then close to complete pooling. This is the case of strongest shrinkage: the observations
of a rock count for little when the model says that rocks do not differ.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 7: a forgotten argument"}

A student fits the NLL of a model with a random intercept per site, but forgets the
argument `random = "u"` in `MakeADFun()`. What does `optim()` then minimise, and what
happens to the estimate of $\sigma_{\mathrm{site}}$?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

Without `random`, the site effects are ordinary parameters, and `optim()` minimises the
joint NLL over them and the other parameters together, which is not a likelihood of the
parameters. As $\sigma_{\mathrm{site}}$ shrinks towards zero with all site effects at
zero, minus the log density of the effects decreases without bound, so the joint NLL has
no minimum and the estimate of $\sigma_{\mathrm{site}}$ runs towards zero. `random = "u"`
integrates the site effects out, and the marginal NLL has a proper minimum.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 8: variance among streams"}

The density of mayfly larvae is described with a random effect per stream and five fixed
effects of stream-level predictors, fitted to eight streams. Why might REML be preferred
for the variance among streams? A colleague then compares models with and without one of
the predictors by the AIC of their REML fits. What is wrong?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

With eight streams and five fixed effects estimated from their deviations, the deviations
look much smaller than they are, and the maximum likelihood estimate of the variance among
streams is likely to be much too small; REML integrates the fixed effects out and reduces
this bias. But the REML likelihood depends on which fixed effects were integrated out, so
models with different fixed effects do not have comparable REML likelihoods. They must be
compared with their maximum likelihood fits.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 9: phenology of observed and new sites"}

A model with a random effect per site describes the date of first flowering of a shrub
against spring temperature at 20 monitored sites. Which curve would you use to predict the
flowering date next year at one of the monitored sites, and which at a site where
monitoring starts next year?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

At a monitored site, the curve with the predicted effect of that site, because its
observations tell us how that site differs from the typical one. At a new site the effect
is unknown, so we use the typical curve, with the range that the distribution of site
effects gives for new sites, which is wider.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 10: parameters of a nestling growth model"}

The growth in mass of nestlings is described by a curve with three parameters, with a
random effect per brood on one of them and Normal variation of the measurements around
the curve of each brood. The model is fitted to 40 broods, each measured several times.
How many parameters $K$ enter its AIC? And why is it not compared with other models by
AICc or BIC?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

$K=5$: the three parameters of the curve, the standard deviation among broods
$\sigma_{\mathrm{brood}}$ and the standard deviation of the measurements
$\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}$. The 40 brood effects are not counted, because they are integrated
out of the marginal likelihood, so together they cost one parameter,
$\sigma_{\mathrm{brood}}$, and $K$ is 5 and not 45. AICc and BIC need the number of
independent observations $n$, which is ambiguous here: the measurements of a brood share
its effect, so they are not independent, but each adds information about the curve of its
brood. The effective number lies somewhere between the 40 broods and the number of
measurements, depending on how large the variance among broods is compared with the
variance within broods.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 11: seed mass of trees"}

The seed mass of 25 trees is modelled with complete pooling, with no pooling (one mean per
tree) and with a random effect per tree. No pooling has the lowest AIC. Should it be
preferred?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

Not by that comparison. The likelihood of no pooling describes new seeds of the same 25
trees, with their means as parameters, whereas the marginal likelihood of the mixed model
describes the seeds of a new tree, whose mean is unknown. The AICs measure predictions of
different things, so they cannot be compared. If the question is about these 25 trees, no
pooling or the predicted effects of the mixed model answer it; if it is about trees of the
species, only the mixed model does.

:::
::::
